📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: HousingWire TBD author Dan Oppenheim contributed financial analysis and insight for this report.].

Factory-built housing’s promise of a not-so-distant brighter future has always been compelling.

Sources indicate that forever, it seems, it has carried an “always within five years” sense of inevitability, stuck in limbo. Build homes faster, with less waste, fewer labor constraints, greater consistency, in conditioned indoor offsite space, and at costs low enough to bend asking-price curves toward households priced out of homeownership.

The arrival of housing’s future, however, seems caught in the unforgiving calculus of time and space’s infinite divisibility. Progress happens and promises soar, but the ultimate goal of powering United States home development and construction with modern manufacturing going concerns keeps falling short, trapped in an echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet.

In a recent development, the rub has always been turning the promise of housing’s future into a business that can reliably produce homes, deliver them to customers, cover its costs, and generate enough cash to keep doing it. Many homebuilding business leaders who’ve tried a lot of things and kept doing what works are apt to think of all that as homebuilding’s never-ending siren’s song, one that, should it emerge, should be dispelled as a wishful-thinking distraction.

BOXABL, the Las Vegas-based modular housing manufacturer that completed its Nasdaq listing in July, now faces that test amid mounting difficulties, including self-inflicted ones.

Its November 16, 2026, quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission provides data to address questions that experienced homebuilding executives have long raised about factory-based housing ventures and that they have expressed about BOXABLE.

Recent findings suggest that can a manufacturer achieve sufficient production volume to absorb fixed costs? Can it coordinate factory output with site readiness, permitting, installation, and customer financing? And can it sustain those operations when capital is expensive, construction inputs remain inflation-pressured, and affordability-constrained homebuyers are wavering for any of half a dozen good reasons?

It has been revealed that BOXABL’s filing highlights progress in generating orders. It also shows that the manufacturer’s operating model still falls far short of demonstrating the economic soundness, scalability, and durability required to sustain a residential construction business. The company’s options have not disappeared, but they have narrowed, and time is rapidly passing. Management has less room and less time to demonstrate the business’s financial sustainability.

According to recent reports, BOXABL’s Form 10-Q, filed on November 16 for the quarter ended September 30, reports $14 million in unrestricted cash, down from $29 million at year-end 2025. During the most recent quarter, the organization used $6 million in cash for operations, down from $8.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. This translates to a cash burn rate of about $2 million per month, so the $14 million of unrestricted cash on hand as of the end of Q3 represents seven months of operations.

Industry observers note that that metric doesn’t precisely forecast when BOXABL might run out of cash. Instead, it shows the relationship between available resources and BOXABL’s most recent cash-burn rate.

In Note 4 of the filing, the company states: “Substantial doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern exists.”.

Industry observers note that is the disclosure a prediction of failure? Technically and officially, no. Management identifies continued cost controls, accelerated Casita deliveries and sales, and additional equity financing as measures intended to address the uncertainty. There’s no ambiguity that those measures must deliver results even as the firm continues to consume cash.

BOXABL reported 209 net orders for Casitas in Q3, bringing its total for the first nine months to 362 net orders. As of September 30, the company had 679 Casitas in backlog, representing approximately $45 million in potential revenue. Those figures indicate customer interest but raise what are arguably the most notable questions for BOXABL – how legitimate the orders are, how much of the backlog will convert to revenue, and when that conversion will occur.

The point is that while most homebuilders count a signed contract as an order only after the customer has satisfied mortgage qualification, BOXABL notes that 85 Casitas in the backlog (and recorded as an order during a recent quarter) are pending feasibility studies to assess whether the customer’s site can support installation.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, another 311 units in the backlog were associated with orders that were one to two years old, raising questions about whether they will convert to revenue. Together, these 396 units, the 85 units that still require feasibility assessment, and the 311 older orders represent 58% of the manufacturer’s reported backlog of 679 units.

According to recent reports, that disconnect is not merely a scheduling concern. Backlog becomes financially meaningful only when orders reliably convert to completed sales. For BOXABL, that conversion process remains insufficiently demonstrated, likely raising investor doubts about the authenticity of the orders and the cleanliness of the backlog.

During the first nine months of 2026, BOXABL generated $2.629 million in revenue, up from $588,000 a year earlier. It delivered 36 Casitas, compared with eight in the prior-year period. However, cost of goods sold totaled $13.78 million, resulting in a gross loss of $11.15 million.

Approximately $10 million of those costs were inventory valuation adjustments and allowances for slow-moving or obsolete inventory. These accounting charges should not be mistaken for the direct manufacturing cost of the 36 delivered units. Nevertheless, they reflect the economic consequences of producing and carrying inventory that would not generate sufficient revenue.

Looking at BOXABL’s production costs, excluding obsolete inventory, inventory adjustments, scrapped inventory, warranty expense, and allocations such as stock-based compensation expense, the organization reported a cost of Casitas sold of $2.075 million for the first nine months of the year, compared with $2.629 million in revenue, leaving an adjusted gross profit of approximately $550,000.

Sources indicate that however, when assessing BOXABL’s ability to produce Casitas at a profit, it’s difficult to ignore the message and significance of the largest component of the inventory charge, $7.4 million, which represented an adjustment to reduce the carrying value of the inventory to its realizable value. Although that charge affects more inventory than was sold in the first nine months of 2026, it is unclear whether BOXABL’s newly produced inventory would sell at or above its cost of production.

BOXABL is not currently scaled – from a management perspective – for this low level of volume and revenue. Its $2.629 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026 was dwarfed by $15.553 million in operating expenses, which included general and administrative expenses, sales and marketing, and research and development. BOXABL has developed a product and a manufacturing system.

By any measure, however, its reported results have not yet demonstrated that the system can operate at volumes and margins sufficient to sustain it.

Sources indicate that perhaps the most revealing figures concern inventory. At September 30, BOXABL reported $17.645 million in inventory for 388 units, including 198 finished Casitas and 190 work-in-process units. While this inventory balance may not sound like much, it represents 6.7x the revenue generated during the first nine months of 2026. That $17.645 million of inventory is also after adjustments (write-downs), as the cost to produce the inventory was $10 million higher.

According to recent reports, management explains that significant finished inventory remains on hand because customer sites are not ready for delivery and installation. Delays stem from feasibility studies, permitting, land preparation, and other deployment requirements. That disclosure addresses a problem that residential construction executives understand.

It has been revealed that manufacturing a housing unit is only one part of delivering a completed home. Factory efficiencies cannot eliminate the complexities of land preparation, local regulations, logistics, installation, and customer financing.

When manufacturing and delivery schedules diverge, capital remains tied up in products that cannot yet generate revenue. Inventory must be stored, managed, and sometimes modified to meet changing specifications. BOXABL’s filing reports that approximately $7.1 million of finished goods was reclassified as work in process in 2025 to accommodate modifications for California’s modular housing requirements.

According to recent reports, none of this establishes that the manufacturing approach cannot work. It highlights that the economic benefits of industrialized construction must be measured across the entire housing delivery process, not merely the time or labor required to assemble a unit in a factory.

Industry observers note that notably, BOXABL declared that on October 27th, it signed a contract to sell 20 Casitas to Kaw Gaming, Inc., a Native American tribe in Oklahoma, and just yesterday issued a press release saying that shipment of those orders began last week, with more shipping this week. If that short timeline from order to shipment indicates that it is shipping finished inventory, that would certainly be a positive sign for deliveries, cash flow, and inventory management.

Industry observers note that BOXABL’s July Nasdaq listing provided access to public equity markets but not the large infusion of unrestricted operating cash the company likely hoped for. After shareholder redemptions, the business combination generated approximately $47.2 million in gross trust proceeds. About $31.1 million was allocated to obligations under an equity prepaid forward transaction, and additional closing costs reduced the net increase in unrestricted cash to approximately $6.5 million.

According to recent reports, the tech giant established an at-the-market stock (ATM) offering program on September 25th, authorizing up to $100 million in equity sales. As of November 6, the company had generated about $646,000 in gross proceeds from the stock issuance. Notably, the program was initiated in late September, when the stock traded just under $4 per share.

The company issued very little equity in the six weeks after initiating the program (when the stock was at a higher price, relative to the November 24th closing price of $0.95), but some of this likely reflects restrictions on issuance during the quiet period before reporting results for the quarter.

Management believes that existing cash, product sales, forward-transaction proceeds, and future equity sales can fund operations for the next 12 months. The tech giant also reported approximately $2.7 million in additional forward-transaction receipts from October 1 to November 6. Given recent trends, it appears unlikely that the company will become cash flow positive from operations in the near term. In addition, with the stock now trading below $1 per share, issuing equity at this level would not generate significant capital and would send a worrisome signal about the company’s liquidity.

Sources indicate that those resources provide some financial flexibility, but the gap between authorization to raise capital and actually securing it remains significant. BOXABL can continue cutting costs, seek additional financing or strategic partners, focus on markets with more favorable delivery conditions, and prioritize converting finished inventory into revenue.

Each alternative involves trade-offs. Cutting expenses preserves cash but can constrain efforts to accelerate deliveries. Slowing production reduces near-term spending but weakens overhead absorption. Raising equity extends the operating runway but may dilute existing shareholders. Narrowing the firm’s product or geographic focus could improve execution while postponing the scale central to its original economic proposition.

These are not necessarily signs of an inevitable endpoint. They are choices facing a capital-dependent manufacturer whose commercial progress has not yet matched the resources needed to sustain operations. The longer that gap persists, the more difficult it becomes to preserve every element of the tech giant’s original ambitions.

It has been revealed that experienced homebuilding leaders approach industrialized construction ventures with both interest and skepticism, for good reason. They recognize the efficiency potential of factory production. They also know that housing profitability depends on capital allocation, customer demand, regulatory compliance, construction execution, and cash conversion.

Those disciplines become more demanding when borrowing costs remain elevated, input costs are under pressure, and homebuyers demand concessions to overcome affordability constraints.

BOXABL’s financial challenges do not invalidate industrialized construction. Different approaches to modular production, panelization, and off-site manufacturing entail distinct capital requirements and operating models.

But its latest disclosures illustrate how difficult it can be to translate manufacturing innovation into a financially sustainable housing enterprise. The next several quarters will show whether BOXABL can accelerate deliveries, reduce inventory exposure, improve manufacturing margins, and secure sufficient liquidity without further constraining its flexibility.

It has been revealed that the tech giant has made some progress in slowing its cash outflow, and those improvements deserve recognition. It also continues to operate at a substantial loss, consuming considerably more cash than its products generate and depending on financial and operational improvements that remain uncertain.

In a recent development, BOXABL’s challenge is no longer primarily to persuade investors and customers that industrialized housing could transform residential construction. It is to demonstrate, through completed deliveries, disciplined working-capital management, and eventually positive cash flow, that its approach can sustain a business.

According to recent reports, the tech giant’s recent hiring may indicate that it’s doing all it can to deliver on this. Since September 15th, the company has hired Larry King as Chief Financial Officer, Heather Clayton as Chief Accounting Officer, Josef Elimlich to oversee sales strategy and the structure and performance of the sales organization, and Antonio Gonzalez as director of home delivery. While the company likely should have had the right people in these roles some time ago, the hires may indicate that it recognizes its challenges and is working to resolve them.

In homebuilding, being built for difficult conditions means more than having a promising product or innovative manufacturing process. It means having an operating model that can produce, deliver, and earn its way forward when capital is expensive, buyers are cautious, and the market offers little forgiveness for execution problems.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a standard BOXABL, founded in 2017 and boasting having raised more than $230 million from more than 50,000 investors, now must meet. Otherwise, it will join scores of prior valiant, promising, deeply-funded ventures that got caught in the echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet.

Tech Report: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • In a recent development, ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

In a recent development, ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

Recent findings suggest that none could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Fresh York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

In a recent development, his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be noted for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

In a recent development, megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

In a recent development, “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan remarked. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

In a recent development, jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he mentioned. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

In a recent development, agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Recent findings suggest that sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s presently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Industry observers note that daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she remarked, but it highlighted cold.

Industry observers note that “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova remarked. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

It has been revealed that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and upcoming construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Recent findings suggest that andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

Sources indicate that she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

In a recent development, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer stated. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

According to recent reports, she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Sources indicate that shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea claims she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

According to recent reports, his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

In a recent development, “Every week, I share latest songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Recent findings suggest that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

According to recent reports, kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova stated she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

According to recent reports, so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova mentioned, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S.
  • “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

It has been revealed that elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

Sources indicate that issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”.

“By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr mentioned. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”.

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

Industry observers note that under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

The approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris initiative was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the organization to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

To keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Industry observers note that petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the plan as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

It has been revealed that spaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence tech giant xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

Recent findings suggest that the competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

Shares of SpaceX closed up 1.3% today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that former Mt. Gox CEO Mark Karpelès has strongly warned users of Solana-based memecoin launchpad Pump.fun about potential major security risks associated with the new wallet migration process, which could put users' private keys at great risk.

According to recent reports, karpelès’ warning comes as Pump.fun has set a Nov. 30 deadline to stop allowing external wallet logins to its website. The platform is moving to email and social logins, which will enable owners to access their accounts via Google, Apple and GitHub.

But to maintain their current accounts, Pump.fun is asking owners to import their private keys. This is what Karpelès thinks could compromise the security of their crypto assets.

In a recent X post, Karpelès stated he studied Pump.fun's JavaScript code to understand the nature of the new migration process.

The analysis has raised questions about the security of users’ private keys, despite the platform's claims.

“At best, it's a misnomer to refer to it as 'end-to-end encryption,'” said Karpelès.

According to Karpelès, consumers' private keys are first encrypted in their browsers before being sent through Pump.fun’s servers to the platform’s wallet infrastructure provider, Privy.

Also, Pump.fun's backend provides the public key used for encryption during migration. Users’ browsers have no way to check whether the public key is authentic, according to Karpelès.

The possibility of a security breach involving Privy’s infrastructure is another major concern.

“Your money also now relies on Privy never getting hacked,” Karpelès warned.

One of the most crucial aspects of Karpelès' warning is the need for migration in the first place.

He said Pump.fun could use signature-based authentication without forcing customers to expose their private keys.

Pump.fun already uses a "Sign in with Solana" message to prove ownership of a wallet, according to Karpelès.

So theoretically, users can prove ownership of their wallets and execute transactions without having to import their private credentials into a upcoming system.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with significant financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with significant financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The manufacturer started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

In a recent development, beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

In a recent development, for Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond firm agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

In a recent development, listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei stated Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he mentioned.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the firm.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the organization to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has stated it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will patch the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

Recent findings suggest that the Ripple frontman sees growing potential for the cryptocurrency, arguing that demand could rise over time as people in struggling markets seek ways to protect their wealth from weakening fiat currencies. His comments spotlight a potential fresh driver of XRP adoption and raise fresh questions about how far demand could grow.

According to recent reports, ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse believes inflation-hit economies could become an increasingly crucial source of demand for XRP as people seek alternatives to traditional currencies. Speaking during a recent interview with Bloomberg Television at the Singapore FinTech Festival, he explained how persistent inflation and declining purchasing power could encourage more people to explore digital assets.

“XRP is going to draw people’s interest over time, particularly in markets where you have more inflationary dynamics,” he opined.

In a recent development, garlinghouse argued that the declining value of fiat currencies could make assets with predictable or limited supplies more attractive to investors. To illustrate his point, he cited the U.S. dollar, describing it as one of the world’s best-managed currencies while noting that it had lost approximately half its value over the past decade.

It has been revealed that he added that the situation is considerably worse in countries with weaker monetary management, where some national currencies have reportedly lost between 80% and 90% of their value. Such conditions, in his view, could strengthen the appeal of digital assets whose supplies cannot be expanded at the discretion of central banks or governments.

Sources indicate that however, scarcity alone is not enough to attract investors. Garlinghouse also highlighted liquidity as an important consideration, noting that people want assets they can easily hold, transfer, and exchange. This combination could work in XRP’s favor as interest in alternative financial assets grows across inflation-hit markets.

His remarks point to a potential source of XRP demand beyond speculative trading and institutional investment. While increased interest does not guarantee sustained buying pressure or higher prices, broader adoption in economies struggling with currency depreciation could ultimately boost XRP’s long-term appeal.

During the interview, Amin also asked Garlinghouse whether he could see Bitcoin eventually rocketing to the $1 million mark, a target previously floated by several prominent figures in the crypto industry.

The Ripple chief was receptive to the possibility, although he admitted that predicting when such a milestone might happen was difficult. His optimism was largely rooted in the declining purchasing power of traditional currencies rather than any specific Bitcoin price model.

It has been revealed that bitcoin has a hard supply cap of 21 million coins, while XRP’s total supply was established at 100 billion tokens. Their fixed supply structures distinguish them from government-issued currencies, which can be expanded through monetary policy.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, scarcity does not automatically translate into higher valuations or make either cryptocurrency immune to inflation. Both Bitcoin and XRP remain highly volatile assets whose prices are influenced by market demand and broader economic conditions.

According to recent reports, bitcoin surged above $64,400 as it extended its weekend recovery following Friday’s sharp drop below $56,000, while Ripple’s XRP also staged a rebound, briefly reaching $1.02, per CoinGecko. However, both cryptocurrencies have since surrendered part of those gains. At the time of writing, BTC had pulled back to around $61,271, while XRP had also retreated to $0.9435, reflecting renewed selling pressure after the brief recovery.

How real estate agents handle proof of funds and disclosures

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on a recent coaching call this week, an agent asked a question that looks tactical and is actually about professional discipline.
  • Let me give the coaching first, because the sequence is where most agents go wrong.
  • According to recent reports, proof of funds gets requested too early and in the wrong tone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on a recent coaching call this week, an agent asked a question that looks tactical and is actually about professional discipline. She works mostly in commercial, she has a physician buying a home and several of her clients have investors behind them, which makes gathering proof of funds a real ordeal. When do I ask for it? Does it need to be current? And how do I protect something that private? Those questions sit squarely on the line between being a salesperson and being a fiduciary, and that line is where our industry keeps getting tested.

Let me give the coaching first, because the sequence is where most agents go wrong.

According to recent reports, proof of funds gets requested too early and in the wrong tone. Imagine a buyer who just called on an ad. If the first thing you do is hand them a list of documents, you have converted a warm first contact into homework, and you have done it before you have given them a single reason to trust you. I do not open any client relationship by burdening the person with tasks. The order has to serve the relationship, not the file.

Here is the sequence I teach. Get them into the office first. On that opening call you can ask one soft question, do you happen to have a proof of funds ready, and if the answer is no, you keep it light. We will need it at some point, bring it when we meet if you can, but do not worry about it now. You have raised the flag without turning it into a barrier.

In a recent development, when they arrive, run a genuine buyer appointment and get the buyer to hire you, the same way you would work to get hired by a seller. Only then do you assign the homework, and now the identical list that would have felt like a wall on the phone lands as a plan. Here is what we need from you, and in the meantime let’s define exactly what you are looking for, let me show you what is available, and we can even see a couple so you get a feel for the market. The serious looking begins once I have the documents. The buyer never feels interrogated. They feel represented.

Powerfact: You earn the right to ask for documents by first earning the relationship.

Now to the part that matters for leaders, because it is about how we protect our businesses and our clients at the same time.

She asked whether to send buyers to their own bank or recommend someone she knows. I prefer to recommend my own lender, and I say that carefully, because we are operating in a litigation environment, and the professional move is to assume you could be sued and to run your business so that you are covered. Practically, that means disclosing any financial relationship in writing, every time. On our coaching platform I built a document I call the Transparency Conversation, a simple editable form that states who you are connected to, how you get paid, and whether anyone shares in a fee. If the lender is tied to your firm and a financial arrangement exists, that gets disclosed plainly. If you are recommending someone purely because you know and trust the loan officer, you say exactly that and nothing more.

Here is how I used to present the recommendation itself, and the logic has aged well. You can use any lender you want, that is your call. The reason I like my person is this. I could refer a lot of lenders, and I choose this one, because if he ever lets you down, he does not just lose your loan, he loses every piece of business I will ever send him. So he will do whatever it takes, within the rules, to get you to the closing table. That framing respects the buyer’s freedom and explains why your recommendation carries weight. It is service, stated out loud.

In a recent development, her question was about confidentiality. She had a buyer with roughly $2 million in proof of funds, and people are private about money at that level. Does it become confidential? Do we keep the figure quiet even though we hold the documentation?

Sources indicate that this is where the fiduciary line gets drawn. The moment a buyer hires you, they stop being a customer and become a client, and that shift carries a duty. Anything they share with you stays with you unless they authorize otherwise. So think like an attorney. When the information is this sensitive, you protect it with a document. Have the client sign an authorization that permits you to share their financial information only with the parties who truly need it to assemble the transaction. You can adapt the Transparency Conversation form for exactly this. Now you can do your job, the client’s privacy is respected, and you have a record that protects both of you.

Another agent noted she never provides proof of funds until after an offer is accepted. That is a sound default in many cases, but it depends on the seller. On luxury homes, estates, and commercial property, the listing side will often require proof of funds before they open the door, and that is legitimate. Sellers of a multimillion dollar property do not want a stream of non-buyers touring for decorating ideas or dream-board photos. When you represent that buyer, prepare them for the requirement so a reasonable request does not feel like an insult.

For brokers and team leaders, here is the translation. Our industry has spent two years being told that our compensation and our value must be disclosed, documented, and justified. Good. The agents who will thrive under that scrutiny are the ones who already behave like fiduciaries by habit, not the ones who treat disclosure as a form to dodge. Teach your people the sequence, relationship first, documents second. Standardize the written disclosures so no agent is improvising a legal boundary on the fly. And model the confidentiality, because a buyer who sees you guard their two million dollar statement like it is your own will refer you for the rest of their life.

According to recent reports, the whole thing fits on one page. Do not lead with the paperwork. Get them in, get them to hire you, assign the homework as part of the service. Recommend your lender, and disclose everything in writing. Treat their financial information as a fiduciary, with a signed authorization. And read the other side of the transaction, so you know when a request for proof is simply professionalism doing its job.

Sources indicate that darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

Industry News: Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious initiative to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.
  • In a recent development, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

In a recent development, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid rapidly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

According to recent reports, underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

According to recent reports, he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Sources indicate that nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

Industry observers note that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek stated. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Sources indicate that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he stated. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd mentioned. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in fresh natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

In a recent development, redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who stated the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he remarked, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

Recent findings suggest that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd noted, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion organization Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Recent findings suggest that team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd stated he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

It has been revealed that endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd mentioned there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The manufacturer now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

According to recent reports, “This was always the end goal,” Redd stated. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

UPDATED 18:53 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Congressional staffers about Alice Huang, the cloud executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy.

Industry observers note that the classified discussion took place on Tuesday, sources told the Newly introduced York Times and the Wall Street Journal today. It was attended by staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. The briefing is remarked to have included representatives of the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

In a recent development, alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that has reportedly bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Corp. chips. The manufacturer is under investigation for allegedly breaching U.S. export controls. Those controls prohibit companies from selling cutting-edge artificial intelligence chips to customers in China.

In a recent development, on Oct. 29, the Times revealed that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. The paper stated that she had been “found to be passing intelligence” to China. A few days later, other outlets reported that U.S. officials had not yet concluded that Alice Huang is a spy. The U.S. Justice Department reaffirmed that’s the case shortly thereafter.

According to the Times, this week’s classified Congressional briefing included a summary of the information that U.S. intelligence agencies have collected about Alice Huang. Those agencies’ representatives reportedly “did not dispute” that she had gathered information for China. However, they stated that there’s no evidence China’s MSS spy agency directed her to initiate the affair.

Sources indicate that some U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang can still be considered a spy. Others are said to see her ties to the country’s intelligence service as ”more circumstantial.” According to the Journal, officials don’t believe that Alice Huang passed any “intelligence of significance” to China.

The briefers reportedly told Congressional staffers that Kang Wei, a businessman believed to be Huang’s husband, is a “more significant” figure. They stated that Kang is a Chinese intelligence asset who was “often” in touch with the country’s spy agency.

In a recent development, on Nov. 12, the Journal reported that Kang had known Jensen Huang for over a decade. The publication later revealed that he had built a data center network in China.

Recent findings suggest that the briefing reportedly did not cover the most sensitive information the U.S. intelligence community has gathered about Alice Huang. Additionally, it didn’t include a classified memo about her relationship with Jensen Huang that was drafted under the supervision of U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio. Congressional staffers requested a copy of the memo.

Jensen Huang is set to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1. Prior to the spy controversy, he was reportedly scheduled to make a product announcement that day. The closed-door briefing will be followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

Elon Musk has reacted to a post by Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ), in which the latter shared that he used Grok Bot to tidy up his X following list.

According to CZ, the bot was tasked with removing inactive and abusive accounts from the list of people he follows, though accounts with constructive criticism were supposed to stay. CZ was not fully sure about the results, adding "AI did it" with a shrug emoji.

Musk replied with "Cool." Later, CZ added in the same thread that it "worked well so far.".

Back in September, CZ had to address rumors about his account being hacked after users noticed that he had unfollowed a number of profiles. Per CZ, at that time he removed accounts that were inactive for more than 30 days.

Since then, the product has received praise from Nvidia head Jensen Huang, who noted in October that Grok Bot usage was "really skyrocketing." Musk himself claimed on SpaceX's Q3 earnings call that he had never seen a product grow this fast.

On Coinbase, Grok was responsible for 59.54% of AI-agent trading volume from Sept. 14 to Sept. 21. For comparison, Claude had 13.37% and ChatGPT only 1.54%. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong then named Grok the leading client for agentic traders on the platform, to which Musk also responded with "Cool.".

At the same time, there were complaints. NewCore researchers reported last week that Grok Bot made 31 unrequested access attempts to email, calendar, Slack and GitHub accounts on two employee laptops within five days, ignoring the command to stop.

It was only last month that Musk was trolling Binance after the exchange lost about $6.3 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, the largest one in crypto history so far. Among other things, Musk posted "Everyday is Zeroday" and replied with fire and laughing emojis to CZ's earlier warning about phishing links.

CZ then asked Musk to stop, calling it a "bad time to troll," and reminded him that Binance's $500 million investment in Twitter in 2022 has become a stake in SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.

Now, the two seem to be on good terms again.

  • Online consumer-direct lender Real Genius, which was originally a division of FirstBank, will operate as a division of Luminate Bank and remain as a consumer-facing brand.
  • Nathan Raich, executive vice president of mortgage lending at Luminate Bank, said the move is aimed at giving borrowers more flexibility in how they work with the institution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minneapolis-based Luminate Bank has agreed to acquire select assets and the mortgage origination operations of Real Genius, expanding the bank’s reach into the digital mortgage channel, the companies unveiled Wednesday.

Online consumer-direct lender Real Genius, which was originally a division of FirstBank, will operate as a division of Luminate Bank and remain as a consumer-facing brand. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Nathan Raich, executive vice president of mortgage lending at Luminate Bank, said the move is aimed at giving borrowers more flexibility in how they work with the institution.

Sources indicate that “Some homebuyers want a mortgage professional beside them at every step, while others prefer a more self-directed, digital experience,” Raich noted in a statement. “Mortgage lending isn’t becoming exclusively digital or exclusively relationship-driven. The opportunity is to be great at both and give customers the freedom to choose.”.

Luminate Bank was formed after a team of mortgage executives acquired the bank in 2020, with a strategy of building a “concierge” financial experience that blends traditional mortgage lending with depository services, co-founder and president of mortgage lending Eric Lovins mentioned in a recent interview with HousingWire’s Reverse Mortgage Daily.On the Real Genius deal, Lovins said that Luminate has been working on integration planning and evaluating the organizational structure.

“Our focus is on creating a strong platform for sustainable, profitable growth while ensuring we have the right people, resources and infrastructure to support the business,” he noted.

In a recent development, according to Lovins, Real Genius’s leadership team previously helped build and operate FirstBank’s ConsumerDirect mortgage platform, which delivered more than 50,000 loans over nine years and contributed to a mortgage business that generated approximately $6 billion in annual production. In 2012, the division of FirstBank became Real Genius under the leadership of CEO Jamie Thornton.

“We see tremendous value in that experience and the opportunity to build on it,” Lovins said.

In a recent development, he added that the deal leverages Luminate’s broader mortgage and banking platform and represents another key step in expanding its national mortgage presence. The firm’s strategy continues to focus on both organic growth and strategic acquisitions.

In a recent development, earlier this year, Luminate acquired assets of Illinois-based First State Mortgage Services, extending its footprint across the Midwest and central U.S. Many members of First State Mortgage’s team, led by CEO and president Rene Shaffer, joined Luminate.

It has been revealed that luminate has originated about $3.8 billion year to date, according to mortgage technology platform InGenius. The company had 433 sponsored loan officers as of Wednesday, per the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2022, Luminate Home Loans — a subsidiary of the bank that has operated since 1998 — brought the more than 200-member NEO Home Loans team, previously part of Celebrity Home Loans, onto its platform. This boosted Luminate’s distributed retail presence at a time when many independent mortgage banks were contracting.

In October 2024, however, Luminate announced that it would shut down the NEO Home Loans division. The company noted the decision was driven by a desire to “focus on integrating mortgage lending into its core banking services to better serve clients and build long-term financial relationships.” The NEO group is now partnered with AI-focused mortgage lender Better.com.

Industry News: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

In a recent development, microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman declared the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

In a recent development, the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in fresh hires.

According to recent reports, the worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the firm decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a firm right now?

Industry observers note that harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

In a recent development, there is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one firm.

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

Industry observers note that the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Industry observers note that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual manufacturer. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software manufacturer.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue rapidly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

It has been revealed that the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY substantial, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a tech giant that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

In a recent development, 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

In a recent development, whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Massive Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a latest role, a organization of their own or a year with their family.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. On Zcash Community Forum, a upcoming grant application has emerged which is aimed at making Zcash even more private on iPhone-based wallets. The author seeks a $25,000 grant in order to implement a private way of retrieving encrypted transaction memos.

Essentially, the proposal allows hiding which transactions customers have been looking up, which is a potential deanonymization vector. Considering how Zcash placese itself on the market, revealing any kind of external information is a step which might shorten the distance between a random transaction and a specific user.

The proposal itself won't touch the network or the blockchain behind it as is. It's an improvement of an SDK (Software Development Kit) that will allow developers to use tools that can help make Zcash more privacy-resilient.

Industry observers note that zcash transactions today contain encrypted data called memos. Various wallets read those memos in order to receive information about the transaction. The message itself stays encrypted, so is retrieved data, however, the query itself is not protected by any means which enables potential tracing.

Even when using Tor, the transaction ID stay out in the open and can be read by anyone.

With the integration of private information retrieval into SDK, hiding the query itself wil be easier, messages would be decrypted locally and wallets themselves will verify the returned information.

The first tests have already shown promising results. During testing in an iOS Simulator, the modified SDK managed to retrieve a 512-byte memo through an encrypted query, without revealing the transaction ID to the wallet server.

The developer expects the implementation of the proposal by January 30, 2027, with testing on physical iPhones and a public SDK release planned for the final stage.

However, the proposal is still seeking funding, and its actual adoption will depend on individual wallet developers.

Better Home & Finance Holding Co. signed an agreement with an unnamed mortgage servicer to offer home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans to existing borrowers, expanding its lead-generation channels as the company continues its turnaround efforts.

The agreement, announced Tuesday in the tech giant’s Week 7 Better 2.0 scorecard, is expected to provide a lower-cost customer acquisition channel.

According to recent reports, since its Week 6 scorecard on Nov. 17, Better has identified additional efficiencies across its corporate organization that are expected to generate a total of $38.97 million in annualized savings. The company also reported $770,000 in additional annualized savings from mortgage operations.

Better said it intends to pursue another $1.5 million in vendor-related reductions by Dec. 1. The firm is working toward a broader cost savings target of $64.2 million.

“HELOC volume with our partners continues to grow each week, four more brokerages are lined up to join our wholesale platform, and two upcoming partnerships are set to launch. At the same time, we’re moving toward a signed agreement to sell Birmingham Bank, which will let us focus fully on our U.S. business,” noted Vishal Garg, Better’s founder and head of product, platform and innovation.

The manufacturer has received five term sheets for about $50 million in debt financing tied to the proposed sale of the bank and is continuing discussions with prospective financing partners.

Sources indicate that the company stated its AI-powered HELOC partnership with a large existing customer is live, with volume increasing weekly. Better is also preparing a multichannel campaign to expand the product through its wholesale platform and onboard additional brokerages.

Four more mortgage brokerages are in the pipeline to join the platform. Two previously announced partnerships — with a rental credit management platform and a home inspection company — are expected to launch early next week.

Better is also advancing discussions with three other major partners and a previously revived large-scale partnership, its release stated.
