📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • exchange and the app demonstrates the balance.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Recent findings suggest that open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app demonstrates the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Recent findings suggest that open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

Sources indicate that the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

Sources indicate that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

In a recent development, for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Recent findings suggest that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

It has been revealed that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks indicates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

Sources indicate that the pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

In a recent development, the SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

It has been revealed that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#213759. Report sheds light on China ties of some US-based Nvidia partners

Report sheds light on China ties of some US-based Nvidia partners

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an investigation has shed light on links between some Nvidia Corp.
  • According to recent reports, the analysis was carried out by C4ADS, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit, at the request of CBS News.
  • Sources indicate that the first focus of the investigation was a San Jose, California-based firm called RiCloud AI Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:13 EST / NOVEMBER 26 2026.

Sources indicate that an investigation has shed light on links between some Nvidia Corp. partners and companies that are based in China or are accused of breaching export controls.

According to recent reports, the analysis was carried out by C4ADS, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit, at the request of CBS News. The outlet published the findings Wednesday evening.

Sources indicate that the first focus of the investigation was a San Jose, California-based firm called RiCloud AI Inc. It’s an Nvidia preferred partner, which means that it can buy the chipmaker’s high-end graphics processing units. Companies with that partner destination also have access to Nvidia’s GPU software and technical support services.

Industry observers note that the investigation determined that RiCloud AI is a unit of Shenzen-based Yuxing InfoTech Investment Holdings Ltd. The latter company’s chief executive reportedly has a degree from a university run by China’s military. Yuxing’s chair, in turn, previously worked at a Chinese tech firm that drew national security scrutiny in Australia.

RiCloud AI recently signed a $120 million deal to lease Nvidia-powered servers to a Taiwanese whiskey tech giant. The latter firm generated just $609,000 in profits last year.

The investigation also looked into a company called Topmost Corp. It’s reportedly linked to a California businessman who was recently indicted for allegedly smuggling GPUs to China.

According to CBS News, Topmost’s website states that it’s an authorized reseller of Nvidia partner 2CRSi Inc. The latter manufacturer makes servers powered by the chipmaker’s GPUs. Last month, it disclosed that it received a grand jury subpoena in connection with a client “we ourselves had reported to the authorities.”.

It has been revealed that the report also noted that California-based Aivres Inc. has exported $3 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to Southeast Asia since 2024. It’s a subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech firm that is on the U.S. Commerce Department’s Entity List. Organizations on the list are subject to trade restrictions.

U.S. regulations prohibit companies from exporting Nvidia’s most advanced GPUs to China. Earlier this month, the Commerce Department closed a loophole that Chinese tech firms used to bypass those restrictions. The tech firms in questions rented access to Nvidia GPUs deployed in data centers outside China.

Some of the data centers used by Chinese companies are in Southeast Asia. On Wednesday, the Financial Times reported that Nvidia had instructed manufacturing partners to stop shipping GPU-equipped servers to four countries in the region. It’s reportedly unclear whether the move is temporary.

It has been revealed that separately, CNBC reported that companies have put an “unusually high” number of Nvidia GPUs up for sale since the Commerce Department announced the fresh restrictions. It’s believed the chips were intended for data centers that are used by Chinese firms. According to the report, thousands of high-end B300 GPUs are among the processors that were put up for sale.

Sources indicate that A latest baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

In a recent development, “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla remarked. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

It has been revealed that to spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

In a recent development, birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has concerns with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and Latest Jersey.

It has been revealed that gangiredla noted the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

According to recent reports, the impossible research burden on newly introduced parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

Recent findings suggest that how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — major metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your organization?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

Industry observers note that that “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our organization has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Industry observers note that most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Industry observers note that most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Industry observers note that across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

According to recent reports, together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

Sources indicate that october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

According to recent reports, NU7 does not introduce a upcoming transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

In a recent development, as of ZecStats' latest revision on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who blueprint to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. People need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

It has been revealed that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

According to recent reports, that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

According to recent reports, the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts said last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, shows that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

According to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

Industry observers note that the green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

Industry observers note that the Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

Recent findings suggest that since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

Industry observers note that the Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Goldman also noted that retail investors have been buying major tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

Industry observers note that the Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

Industry observers note that in the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal people that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

In a recent development, microsoft aims to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the firm’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

In a recent development, that’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Recent findings suggest that why Microsoft is doing it: The company remarked putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday owners, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft declared Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

According to recent reports, rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

According to recent reports, reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent manufacturer, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist customers may end up back with the people who built it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Altair Semiconductor Ltd., a supplier of wireless networking chips for connected devices, today announced that it has raised $100 million in funding.
  • According to recent reports, maverick Silicon led the Series A round.
  • Connected devices such as wearables and industrial sensors transmit their data traffic via the same carrier infrastructure as smartphones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:38 EST / NOVEMBER 26 2026.

Altair Semiconductor Ltd., a supplier of wireless networking chips for connected devices, today announced that it has raised $100 million in funding.

According to recent reports, maverick Silicon led the Series A round. It was reportedly joined by Pitango, which invested $50 million in Altair when it spun out of Sony Corp. earlier this year. The Japanese electronics giant is said to have retained a stake.

Connected devices such as wearables and industrial sensors transmit their data traffic via the same carrier infrastructure as smartphones. However, they access that infrastructure in different ways. Connected devices using specialized, low-power network protocols to exchange data with each one and to upload readings to cloud-based backends.

Altair’s flagship modem chip, the ALT1550, supports several such protocols. The most advanced technology in the lineup is the 5G NR eRedCap protocol, which uses 5G networks to transmit data. It consumes significantly less power than a standard smartphone connection and can transmit up to 233 megabits per second.

In a recent development, the ALT1550 also supports two alternative protocols called LTE-M and Cat 1bis. Both use 4G network infrastructure, which is more widely available than the latest 5G hardware. LTE-M can process up to 1 megabits per second, while Cat 1bis is ten times faster and uses more power.

In a recent development, the chip combines a transceiver that picks up and generates radio signals with a baseband processor. That’s a chip specifically optimized for wireless networking tasks. It’s supported by an onboard memory pool, power management circuits and a module that can connect to a satellite when there’s no cell tower nearby.

The ALT1550 is one of several chips offered by Altair. An earlier module, the ALT1255, supports a network protocol called NB-IoT that uses even less power than LTE-M and Cat 1bis. It’s designed for devices that only transmit data every few weeks or months. The ALT1255 provides additional power savings by deactivating many of its features when it’s not in use.

Industry observers note that altair indicates that its silicon can be found in millions of devices. Utilities use it to power smart meters, which automatically transmit usage data to the cloud and thereby remove the need for manual readings. Delivery companies can use Altair chips to track the location of their trucks. The manufacturer’s modules also power medical devices, street lights and a wide range of other systems.

Altair will use its fresh funding round to kick off the mass production of its flagship ALT1550 chip. Additionally, the company plans to develop new networking products and grow its international presence.

It has been revealed that vitalik Buterin is taking Ethereum’s decentralization philosophy down to the silicon level. The Ethereum co-founder published a deep dive into open-source chip design today, covering everything from transistor architecture and manufacturing to hardware security. His central argument? It could have implications far beyond Ethereum, and computing hardware shouldn’t remain a proprietary black box.

Recent findings suggest that could Ethereum eventually move beyond blockchain infrastructure and build its own hardware ecosystem? Vitalik’s latest exploration makes that prospect an interesting thought experiment, particularly as Nvidia dominates the computing industry.

In a recent development, vitalik’s argument starts with a familiar problem in crypto: trust. Software can be audited, code can be published, and blockchain transactions can be independently verified. Hardware, however, remains considerably harder to inspect.

Recent findings suggest that A chip can contain hidden vulnerabilities or malicious modifications that customers cannot easily detect. Even a secure wallet application cannot guarantee safety if the hardware underneath it has been compromised. This has happened recently with Ledger, and Ledger is not the only one, with Trezor and other hardware wallets being recently compromised.

“Not your silicon, not your keys.” – Vitalik put the problem bluntly.

Recent findings suggest that the phrase extends crypto’s self-custody mantra into the physical computing layer. Owning private keys might not mean much if consumers cannot trust the hardware handling them.

This is why Vitalik argues that “the hardware layer must be open for participation and tinkering too.” He wants hardware designs to become accessible to developers, researchers, and independent auditors, allowing them to examine and modify components rather than blindly trusting manufacturers.

It has been revealed that this could eventually create opportunities for Ethereum hardware focused on security, cryptographic computing, and decentralized infrastructure. Ethereum validators, hardware wallets, and zero-knowledge proof systems all depend on computing components that users need to trust.

In a recent development, vitalik acknowledges that open-source hardware faces performance limitations. Advanced chip manufacturing remains expensive and tightly controlled, leaving open designs behind the industry’s most sophisticated commercial processors.

Sources indicate that yet that trade-off might not matter for every workload. Vitalik writes that “Secure hardware may be 10x less efficient or more” while still being sufficient for many computing needs. That’s a striking contrast to an industry obsessed with squeezing more performance from increasingly expensive chips.

Industry observers note that specialized silicon designed for cryptographic operations, privacy-preserving computing, secure data processing, or decentralized networks could benefit from open designs. Developers could modify the architecture, researchers could inspect the circuitry, and manufacturers could compete to produce chips from publicly available specifications.

Sources indicate that ethereum already has an extensive developer community experimenting with cryptography and distributed computing. Extending that culture into silicon could give the ecosystem a foothold in hardware without immediately challenging Nvidia’s AI infrastructure.

The ambition could be less about building another GPU giant and more about creating a competing hardware philosophy.

In a recent development, its greatest strength has been building infrastructure around open participation rather than centralized ownership. If that philosophy eventually reaches the silicon powering modern computing, Ethereum could find itself competing in an industry few would have expected.

Recent findings suggest that are Ripple’s XRP, Cardano (ADA), and Polygon (POL) losing their appeal among crypto investors in 2026? Ben Simpson, founder of crypto investment platform Collective Shift, has named all three among six altcoins he states he wouldn’t touch with a 10-foot pole, citing concerns ranging from weak network activity and questionable valuations to intensifying competition. His blunt assessment raises fresh questions about which altcoins have the strongest fundamentals to survive the increasingly competitive crypto market.

In his post on X, Simpson acknowledged XRP’s role in enabling near-instant, inexpensive payments on the XRP Ledger but argued that the token lacks a compelling mechanism for capturing the value generated by Ripple’s business growth.

Industry observers note that XRP enables fast, low-cost payments on the XRP Ledger.My glitch with XRP is it's "value capture".When a business grows, I want to see how that success benefits the token I'm holding. In this case, there is none. Ripple can grow its revenue, but holders don't receive those….

Recent findings suggest that his main concern is that Ripple’s commercial success does not necessarily translate into direct financial benefits for XRP holders. Even as the San Francisco-headquartered firm expands its revenue and boosts its payment operations, investors do not receive a share of those profits.

Recent findings suggest that he also pointed out that Ripple does not use its business earnings to buy back XRP, a mechanism that could potentially create additional demand for the token. For Simpson, the absence of both profit-sharing and a buyback program makes it difficult to establish a direct link between Ripple’s growing business and XRP’s price in the long term.

He considers these shortcomings significant enough to keep XRP off his investment list, despite the network’s payment capabilities.

According to recent reports, simpson also expressed reservations about Cardano, arguing that its adoption level does not justify its market valuation. Although ADA powers a blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications, he believes the network is generating relatively little economic activity compared with its overall market size.

To support his argument, Simpson pointed to Cardano’s fee generation, claiming that the network collected just $140,000 in transaction fees over a 30-day period despite ADA carrying a market capitalization of approximately $7.5 billion.

It has been revealed that for him, the disparity raises questions about whether Cardano is attracting enough users and developers to sustain its valuation. He believes a blockchain with such a substantial market capitalization should demonstrate considerably stronger usage and demand for its services.

It has been revealed that ultimately, Simpson’s concern is that Cardano needs to translate its technological ambitions and established ecosystem into greater real-world activity. Without a meaningful increase in network usage, he appears unconvinced that ADA offers an attractive investment proposition.

Sources indicate that polygon also made the list, with concerns centered on the growing competition in Ethereum’s scaling ecosystem. Although POL supports a network designed to make transactions faster and cheaper, the increasing number of competing blockchain solutions has made it harder for Polygon to maintain a distinctive advantage.

Simpson’s concern is that newer networks are offering similar benefits, including lower transaction costs and faster processing speeds, leaving Polygon with fewer obvious ways to differentiate itself.

With several projects competing for developers, users, and blockchain activity, POL faces the challenge of proving why it deserves a place ahead of its rivals.

Beyond XRP, Cardano, and Polygon, three other cryptocurrencies also fell short of Ben Simpson’s investment criteria: Sui (SUI), Ronin (RON), and Dogwifhat (WIF). Unlike his concerns about the first three crypto projects, his reservations about these tokens stem largely from changing investment convictions, disappointing adoption, and excessive reliance on market hype.

It has been revealed that sui was among the projects Simpson previously held before changing his investment outlook. The high-speed blockchain is designed to support decentralized applications and transactions, but he eventually dumped his SUI holdings at a loss of between 20% and 30% after his investment thesis changed. He did not elaborate on the specific developments that prompted his decision.

Ronin was another project he abandoned after its growth failed to match his expectations. Initially attracted by the potential of blockchain gaming, the pundit bought into the network, which uses RON for transaction fees and staking. However, the anticipated expansion in gaming adoption did not materialize as he had hoped, prompting him to exit the position relatively rapidly. He argued that strong sector potential means little without meaningful retail participation.

In a recent development, WIF, meanwhile, represented a different kind of investment mistake. Simpson admitted that his decision to buy the Solana-based meme coin was driven largely by hype rather than underlying fundamentals. After his investment thesis changed, he sold his holdings to limit further losses.

His experience with WIF appears to have reinforced his preference for cryptocurrencies backed by stronger fundamentals rather than speculative excitement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.
  • On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.
  • According to recent reports, circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

According to recent reports, circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Industry observers note that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It claims: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle unveiled in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide claims "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide states "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

Sources indicate that the migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

The main text above it notes something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small problem, but the timing makes this one more serious.

In a recent development, many developers now ask AI assistants to write or revision integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

Recent findings suggest that for teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

It has been revealed that for Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

Sources indicate that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#213747. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1016 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the organization acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Industry observers note that testing that more closely replicates the manufacturer’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company indicates it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

Industry observers note that the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

Recent findings suggest that the final report doesn’t say what the July patch was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

In a recent development, third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

In a recent development, how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

Sources indicate that the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Industry observers note that once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft states it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also prepares to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Sources indicate that some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

Sources indicate that the report also confirms what Microsoft mentioned the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the firm states, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

Stellar recorded $207.2 million in tokenized funds in the seven days to November 22, reaffirming continued institutional interest in the blockchain.

The RWA Foundation shared data in a post using figures from Token Terminal showing that Stellar ranked among the top blockchains in tokenized fund growth in the seven days from November 15 to November 22, 2026. Stellar recorded $207.2 million: Franklin Templeton added $108.0 million and Spiko added $68.2 million.

Recent findings suggest that .@injective led tokenized fund growth this past week. @StellarOrg had a good week also. https://t.co/7Ip2oK6c1X.

This means Stellar continues to grow in tokenized assets, a major highlight of strong growth in Q3, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that real-world assets tokenized on Stellar amounted to $4.1 billion at the end of Q3 2026, up 36% from Q2 and up 548% from Q3 2025. Two assets drove the bulk of the quarter’s growth: Tradable’s new tokenized private credit and continued inflows into the Spiko Amundi overnight swap fund.

In a recent development, in late August 2026, Stellar held more tokenized non-US government debt than any other blockchain, with about $490 million in sovereign instruments. These included Spiko’s euro Treasury bill fund, Mexican CETES and Brazilian Tesouro bonds through Etherfuse, South Korean Treasury bonds, and a Marshall Islands digital sovereign bond.

Stellar has widened access to tokenized funds in the United States, Europe and Asia. Franklin Templeton’s BENJI has been on Stellar since 2021. In August 2026, the SEC's Division of Investment Management issued a no-action letter confirming that the Franklin Templeton's registered mutual funds and ETFs may use BENJI for cash management. This expands the set of institutions permitted to hold it. Franklin Templeton made a similar move in Europe, registering 'grBenji' as a Luxembourg UCITS share class for third-party distribution, now live on 21X.

In a recent development, in Asia, Marketnode confirmed in August that it will offer funds from BNY Investments on Stellar, with Marketnode acting as the tokenization and distribution platform. Together, these developments expand access to tokenized funds on Stellar for institutions in the United States, Europe and Asia.

State Street Investment Management and Galaxy brought their Onchain Liquidity Sweep Fund to Stellar in September 2026.

  • But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual latest headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line.Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance.

Recent findings suggest that but demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy.

But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.”.

Industry observers note that budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already mentioned the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034.

Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected demand. More than 1.1 million beneficiaries in the U.S. have signed up for discounted GLP-1s under a pilot introduced this year, allowing patients to access the drugs for reasons other than Type-2 diabetes.

According to recent reports, “On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18 billion to the deficit by 2034. This is roughly 0.9% of the annual deficit, but a much smaller share of GDP, only about 5bps. The cumulative cost over 2026-2034 comes to around $107bn, about three times greater than the CBO’s estimate,” Zwemmer wrote.

According to recent reports, from a macroeconomic perspective, there are also benefits to the government in supporting access to these medications. Zwemmer notes that up to 480,000 more Americans could be working by 2030 thanks to improved health. This would contribute a meaningful lift to payrolls and taxable incomes in a labor force shrinking due to aging and lower immigration.

Individual households that use GLP-1s could also see changes in their personal finances.

It has been revealed that A 2024 study by Cornell and Numerator found that households with at least one GLP-1 user reduced their grocery spending by 5.3% within six months of adoption. Most categories saw spending declines, but the largest reductions were concentrated in calorie-dense, processed categories, including a 10.1% decline in savory snacks.

Industry observers note that the change in consumer behavior is so marked that GLP-1s are helping “keep a lid on food inflation,” Oxford Economics added. Zwemmer writes: “We estimate that GLP-1-using households will reduce their annual spending on food both at home and away from home by a combined $500.”.

Industry observers note that zwemmer also notes that some of those funds may be diverted into buying upcoming wardrobes, highlighting that new starters on GLP-1s are likely to spend $200 on refreshing their clothes. The U.S. economist added: “Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 million users entering 2027, this would translate to an $8bn uplift in apparel spending next year.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The past weeks have seen the broad crypto ETF market face consistent withdrawals from investors, causing Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, and others to record steady outflows since October.

While the negative trend has continued, Solana has just taken over the leadership in the broad ETF market after recording its first inflow in a while.

Latest data from SosoValue demonstrates that while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP ETFs have continued to struggle with consistent weekly outflows, Solana has just beaten the trend after it finally ended a six-week streak of consecutive weekly outflows.

Notably, the data indicates that Solana spot ETFs have recorded a net inflow of $4.38 million over the week.

Although the net amount of capital received by the ETFs appears decent, it is significant considering the growing crypto market weakness.

While this marks an end to the Solana ETFs' six-week outflow streak, this is the first positive weekly performance they have recorded since October 9.

Further data shows that Bitcoin spot ETFs suffered the largest withdrawals as investors pulled out about $1.79 billion during the same period.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the company stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

It has been revealed that microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. Plus, we weigh who from Microsoft could lead Nvidia, and the GeekWire trivia challenge goes back to 1997.

The enterprise licence and PayGo on x402 run on the same software and the same 84 million barcodes. gtinfetch.ai holds the barcodes in full on Microsoft Azure in France, Singapore and the United States, with redundancies on Amazon Web Services (AWS). gtinfetch.ai is live on Model Context Protocol (MCP) at mcp.gtinfetch.ai/mcp.

The Fastest Shift in FMCG and Retail on Record.

In 2024, shopping with AI was a curiosity: a few hundred million people used AI at all. In the fourth quarter of 2026, three billion people use AI, and more than half of consumers shop with AI. The change took 24 months and reached fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) and retail first.

FMCG and Retail Now Run AI Agents. Their Product Data Is Not Ready.

Shoppers moved to AI first. Brands and retailers are now building AI agents to meet AI shoppers, on product data that was never made for AI agents.

In a recent development, the same product carries a different description in every system. An AI agent that matches on words can pick the wrong size, the wrong pack or the wrong maker. The barcode is the one identifier that the brand, the retailer and the AI agent already share.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise software giant SAP SE is reportedly planning to lay off at least 10,000 employees, or over 9% of its workforce.
  • Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructuring initiative is still subject to change.
  • According to the publication, SAP and a labor council in its home country of Germany have negotiated an “employment guarantee” that will run through 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:20 EST / NOVEMBER 26 2026.

Enterprise software giant SAP SE is reportedly planning to lay off at least 10,000 employees, or over 9% of its workforce.

Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructuring initiative is still subject to change.

According to the publication, SAP and a labor council in its home country of Germany have negotiated an “employment guarantee” that will run through 2028. That may mean the layoffs will mainly affect employees in other markets. The report indicates that SAP’s product, engineering and sales units are expected to see the largest cuts.

Executives have reportedly also asked other departments to find cost reduction opportunities.

The reported restructuring push follows a banner quarter for SAP. The company’s sales and adjusted profit both topped analyst expectations. Its €24.11 billion cloud contract backlog, a measure of future revenue, also came in ahead of the consensus estimate.

Recent findings suggest that the planned layoffs are said to be connected to SAP’s efforts to integrate more artificial intelligence features into its products. The company is best known for its ERP, or enterprise resource planning, software. Enterprises use it to automate a long list of backoffice tasks and share data between teams. SAP also sells cloud services for other use cases such as sales automation and customer support.

In a recent development, at a May user conference, the company introduced an AI interface called Joule Work for its applications. SAP notes that the tool will enable workers to centrally access its products instead of navigating multiple screens.

In a recent development, joule Work made its debut alongside a suite of AI agents dubbed Joule Assistants. According to SAP, they will use over 200 subagents to automate repetitive business tasks. Another latest offering, Industry AI, will automate sector-specific workflows.

The report that SAP is preparing for job cuts doesn’t come as a complete surprise. Last week, Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam told attendees of an investor event that the organization expects its headcount to decline. Additionally, two of the software maker’s six directors will reportedly leave in connection with its shift to a more AI-centric strategy.

In a recent development, it’s unclear when the job cuts will take place. According to Bloomberg, SAP historically confirmed workforce reduction programs in January. The software maker took that route with its last major restructuring initiative, which saw it axe about 10,000 roles in 2024. The initiative cost about €3 billion.

The company remarked in a statement that “SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.
  • It has been revealed that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move.
  • The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

It has been revealed that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

According to recent reports, proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration blueprint and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It demonstrates how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:.

Sources indicate that it also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 demonstrated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

According to recent reports, mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

Sources indicate that the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC indicated almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

Sources indicate that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Recent findings suggest that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

In a recent development, at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

In a recent development, proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence reveals what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

According to recent reports, the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#213738. Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1263 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t.
  • But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded, with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.
  • In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output, 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947.

But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded, with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.

In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards.

Recent findings suggest that the consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon, the country’s largest company by revenue, has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion.

Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages.

Sources indicate that “When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time employees have access to health care from their first day—at only $5 per week with $5 copays for employee-only coverage—and 74% of our regular full-time employees are enrolled in an Amazon health insurance plan, well above the 65% private-sector take-up rate for full-time workers,” she said in a statement. “We challenge other large retailers to provide the same Day 1 comprehensive health care benefits that we do.”.

Walmart and FedEx saw similar increases in the number of workers taking federal assistance, as did ride-share and delivery companies.

Sources indicate that kathryn Larin, director for education, workforce, and income security issues at GAO, told Fortune the data illustrates that the Americans taking advantage of social safety net programs today are overwhelmingly in the workforce, with most working full-time. The income threshold for SNAP eligibility is about 130% of the poverty line, suggesting that despite many of these workers clocking in at their jobs, they still don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs.

“What this analysis really points to is the large number of people who have very low incomes and continue to have very low income,” Larin said. “I mean, these are families that are really barely able to make ends meet, and yet they are working, and they are working a lot.”.

In a recent development, diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, recently warned of the hidden consequences of a shrinking labor share, particularly that despite economic indicators suggesting the economy is stable, most Americans are facing an ongoing affordability crisis. KPMG found in February that since 1982, corporate profits as a share of U.S. GDP increased from 8% to 15.85%. During that same period, employee compensation as a share of U.S. GDP shrank from 66.6% to 61.9%.

In a recent development, “This chart from my recent Economic Compass still haunts me,” Swonk mentioned in a social media post at the time. “A friend refers to it as the ‘revolution chart,’ which [is] disturbing but telling. Inequality fuels social and economic instability.”.

This trend has been about 50 years in the making, according to Anna Stansbury, an assistant professor of work and organization studies at the MIT Sloan School of Management.

Recent findings suggest that fewer workers in the U.S. are represented by unions—20.1% of U.S. workers in 1983 compared to 10.0% in 2025—giving them fewer opportunities to bargain for salaries and benefits, she noted. But more so, Stansbury blames the fissuring of the workplace, or the breakdown of the employer-employee relationship. In the past, the typical employer-employee relationship would be that of direct employment: A worker for a firm does their work at the company they are employed by. For example, a large bank like Bank of America used to employ a janitor to clean its offices.

But “in more and more cases, that’s not actually people’s experience of the workplace, particularly in lower middle-income jobs,” Stansbury told Fortune.

In a recent development, instead, large workplaces like retailers and banks hire gig workers or subcontractors to complete jobs once done by direct employees: Companies hire a security provider, which employs a security guard to work outside that large company’s office. Delivery drivers are contract workers, not full-time employees.

According to recent reports, as a result, companies don’t have to provide those workers equity or benefits. If a subcontractor violates labor law, the firm contracting them is not liable. In the meantime, these large companies are not only saving money on benefits, but are also getting to argue that they are increasing efficiency by not spending resources on workers whose roles are not directly driving revenue, Stansbury explained. A bank should employ bankers, not janitors, to get the most bang for its buck, the thinking goes.

Brent Neiman, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago, said he believes AI has been the key driver of diminishing labor shares. In a New York Times op-ed, he argued the technology’s productivity promises pose the greatest threat to wages.

“Anyone who has used ChatGPT can see how much work now done by people could soon be done by technology,” he wrote.

Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok has already observed a correlation between AI adoption and lowered wages. In a white paper published in July, he and economist Sania Edlich found that among 321 occupations between 2015 and 2025, jobs with high exposure to AI saw a 6.7% decline in real wage growth after 2023 (following the wide release of ChatGPT), despite no employment changes, suggesting that while AI is not displacing jobs, it is associated with compressed wages. In other words, companies are seeing increases in productivity, but are using those increases as a cover to raise prices, while keeping wages stagnant.

Stansbury has a slightly different theory about AI. While the technology could begin to have an aggregate impact on the labor market, it’s still too early to say whether today’s shrinking labor share is part of a broader economic cycle, or if it’s a secular event, she stated.

According to recent reports, unexpected inflation spikes, like what is at the moment happening, are usually associated with poorer real wages. If inflation is less volatile in the coming years and wage growth recovers, today’s trend of shrinking labor share could turn out to be cyclical, Stansbury said.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, Stansbury noted, a tightening labor market should increase labor share, and the labor market is already relatively tight. If inflation stabilizes, employment remains narrow, and the labor share increases, it will be a sign of an economic cycle completing itself. A bigger problem will be if wage growth stays low even if inflation improves and the labor market stays tight.

“If those two things happen and the labor share continues to fall,” she said, “then it would suggest that there’s actually been a secular shift, a secular acceleration in the downward trend.”.
